First, **what exactly failed?**  
Write it down, plain English. Was it the code, the data, the logic, the timing? Sometimes it’s a typo, sometimes it’s the whole damn schema. If it’s just one line, maybe it’s a fluke. If the whole table won’t load, that’s not a fluke.

Next, **how did it break? Why?**  
Did the error pop up right after that change, or was it there before? Was it something I changed, or something I didn still’t fix? If it’s only after I swapped out the new merge script for the old one, maybe I just swapped the paths wrong. If the error started showing up after the whole new schema went in, that’s a sign the schema probably shouldn’t be there.

Then, **how many times has it happened?**  
Once? Maybe a fluke. Twice, in the same place? That’s a pattern. If it’s three times in a row after the new module went in, that’s a sign the module’s wrong.

I also check the **logs**—see if the same line is red again, or if something else is off in the next cell. If it’s just one cell, maybe the filter’s off. If the whole batch is wrong, that’s not a setting.

Ask: **is this the only thing that changed?**  
If I updated the API key and it blows up, it’s not the query. If I changed the join, that’s the only thing that could have gone wrong. If the server’s down, it’s not the code.

If I can’t tell, I break it apart. I run the old version, I run the new part by itself. I check the old code in the old version, the new code in the new version. If the old one works and the new one doesn’t, it’s the new code. If both fail, it’s something shared.

If I have to roll it back anyway, I leave a note and fix the merge. If I can’t, I keep the old one and patch the new one with a comment. Only when I’ve checked every comma, every bracket, every space, I call it done.

So, basically:  
**If the error is exactly where the change was, and nothing else looks right, I trust it.  
If it’s somewhere else, or it started after the change went in, I start looking at the new stuff.  
If it’s everywhere, I go back to the old.  
If it’s only sometimes, I split it in half and see which half is breaking.**

That’s how I try not to lose a night to a stupid comma.

When something goes wrong, I don’t just check the box that it’s broken—I want to understand why it broke and if it could have been seen coming. My approach to the post-mortem is methodical and purposeful, so we don some shoes we didn’t want to step in. Here’s how I do it:

First, I grab the full error trace and the exact moment it started. I look at the logs, the stack traces, the inputs, the outputs—everything that’s written. But I also look at what wasn’t written, because silence can be as loud as a scream. I check the environment, the network, the secrets, the permissions. I even ask myself: was it in the code or was it in the setup? Sometimes the config is the real villain.

Then I talk to everyone who was near it. I send the right questions, not just the obvious ones. I want to know what felt off before it became a fire. Did someone skip a step? Was the test green last night? Did a pull request slip through? I keep the chat open until someone says something that doesn, even if it’s “I thought it was fine.” That’s the first clue sometimes.

I draw the timeline on a whiteboard, every change, every merge, every deploy. I color in the green bits and the red. I look for patterns—was it just this one, or was it waiting to happen for three days? I check the previous three months. I check the last merge. I check the last commit after lunch. I want to see if I’m looking at a storm or just a drizzle.

After I have the facts, I write it all down. Not just the what, but the why. I tag the people who were in the right lane and the ones who weren’t. I make a list of fixes and a list of never-go-again. Then I circle back to the boss and say, “We’ll dry it out, but next time we check the river upstream.” I don’t let it drown the next week. I fix what’s broken, but I also make sure it doesn’t flood again.

And I keep the notes. Not just in the ticket, but in my head. Because the next time something like this happens, I want to know why before the water gets up to my knees.

question: When repeated failures occur in the same area, at what point do you conclude the problem is systemic rather than situational?
baseline: When the same errors keep popping up despite clear feedback and corrections, it signals a systemic issue—like a misunderstanding of rules or flawed processes—rather than a one-off slip. At that point, I recommend addressing the root cause, whether through training or revising guidelines, instead of just fixing symptoms.

Great question—it’s a classic line in maintenance and reliability. Deciding if a problem is *situational* or *systemic* after repeated failures in the same spot is about finding the pattern, not just the one time.

Here’s how you know it’s not just a fluke:

**Situational failure:**  
One bolt stripped, one gasket leaked, one wire came loose. Each time it was different, random, maybe a loose fastener someone missed. You fix it, it works for a week, then it’s back again, but not the same spot.

**Systemic failure:**  
Three times, the *same* O-ring on the same joint, same seal, same pressure reading. It’s always the left upper seal, and after you fix it, it fails again an hour later. Or the same motor, same voltage, same code. That’s the pattern. That’s the system telling you something’s wrong with the design, the training, the installation, the material, the environment—*not* just a loose bolt this time.

**The rule of thumb:**  
If you check the same spot, same part, same setting, same everything, three times in a week—no matter what you changed—then you stop asking “what’s wrong here this time?” and start asking “why does it keep happening here?” That’s the sign the system’s broken.

**The chart’s the same:**
- One, maybe two, you call it a coincidence.
- Three, same spot, same story, same fix, same fails again—then you lock it down as a system.

You don’t need a report or a form, just the same, same, same. That’s the rule. If the universe doesn’t care where you put the new seal, then the seal’s broken for everyone.

So, three the same, and you start looking for the process, not the mess. That’s when it’s systemic.

Then I talk to whoever needs to know. If I can, I get the right person to sign off that we did it right, even if it’s not the color they wanted. If I can’t get that, I explain exactly what happened and why. If we can’t ship what’s right, I show what we have and what we’d have to do to fix it, with the new time it’d take. If it’s a repeat, I start asking if we can change the process so it never happens again. Maybe the spec was wrong from the start, or the date was a lie. I keep my notes and my screenshots, because if I say I did it right, I have proof. And next time, I’m not letting it go through until I know it’s right.

If it’s my own work and I let it slip through, I own it. I fix it, and I tell the person I can’t promise it’s perfect next time, but it’ll be better. I don’t let it eat me for weeks. I learn what I missed and I check three times before I call it done next time.

Here’s how I think about it:

**1. Make the bending branches as big as they can be.**  
If you wait for the roots to grow thick before you even show a bud, you’ll be digging for years and nobody will know why. So I try to make the visible part strong and obvious. If the leaves look wrong, the branches don it first. If the stem’s crooked, the whole thing tilts. That’s the only way folks notice anything’s changed. You can’t hide the wrong shape in the air.

**2. But I check the roots anyway.**  
Every time I see the branches right, I know it’s because the roots were right last year. I mark the soil, I check the water, I count the days the ground stays wet. The good days under the dirt are what make the next year’s branches right. If I don’t know where the roots are, I’ll be digging the wrong hole next year.

**3. I keep both maps.**  
I keep a notebook for the days I don’t see anything, the times I think I did it wrong. I mark them anyway. Then when the season comes back and the branches are right, I remember why I kept the notes. That’s when I know the roots were right.

**4. Tell the folks who can’t see the roots.**  
I say it every year: “See how the leaves are straight? That’s because the ground was right last winter. You don’t see that, but it’s everything.” I have to say it, or next year it’ll be wrong again.

So, you can’t just trust what you can see. You have to keep the map for the part you can’t. And you have to keep saying it, even when nobody’s listening. That’s how you know you’re building the right thing, even if you can’t prove it yet.

That’s how I keep the roots from becoming ghosts.

I start with at least two days, but usually three. That’s before I even look at the dependencies. It’s for things going wrong that I can’t see yet—like someone out sick, a file that vanishes, a step that takes twice as long because of some stupid little detail.

But then I break it down by task. For each major chunk, I check the steps, see where the gaps are, and add another day for every two things that have to wait on each other. If three things have to line up, I add two days. If the whole chain could stall if one person’s off, I double it. It’s not pretty, but I can’t afford to be wrong.

After that, I look at the whole map again. If there’s a chain of three hand-offs, I add another day just in case the second person’s gone. I never round up to the next hour—every minute counts when you’re chasing it.

Sometimes it’s not a real change, it’s just someone else yelling louder. Double-check the new priority with the person who raised it. If it’s legit, then we move on.

**2. Accept it.**  
I know it stings. But if the boss or the client says “no, this is what’s going up now,” I stop. I don it on the list, mark the old thing as “not done yet,” and start over. It’s not my fault the sky turned purple today.

I always ask, “what’s the new rule this time?” and make sure I remember it. If I’m moving something up, I check what I dropped and see if I can save a line or a screenshot somewhere, just in case. But I don’t pretend the old stuff was right.

**4. Tell the people.**  
If I’m dropping something, I update the shared doc and send a quick note: “A is out, B is in now.” That way nobody’s looking for A when it’s supposed to be G. I don’t make a big deal about it, but I don’t erase it either.

**5. I keep my head.**  
I know what I let go of. If I can’t sleep over it, I log it and move on. If I have to roll it back later, I know why and I know who to ask. Letting it haunt me is just another thing I can’t control.

**6. Next time, I check the list twice.**  
I make a habit of looking at the top three things before I lock anything down. That way I don’t get caught dropping the wrong thing again.

---

**1. The “Why” Matters More Than the “What”**
If I’m making something just to check the box, I’ll keep going until it’s perfect. But if the reason I’m doing it is because someone else needs to know, or I have to trust it, then I start looking for the first place it could trip me. That’s when I ask: *If I hand this in now, what’s the worst thing that could happen? Can I live with it, or does it eat me for a week?

---

**2. The Same Mistake Twice**
If I fix the same stupid little thing three times and it just keeps popping up again, I know I rushed it. But if I fix it once and it’s gone, maybe it’s done. That’s the difference between a patch and a real fix.

---

**3. The Simplest Way to Forget It’s Even There**
If I can’t even see it anymore, or it’s just background noise, then it’s done. If I have to double-check every step just to remember what I did yesterday, that’s a sign I need to lock it down.

---

**4. The Next Person Would Know**
If I could explain it to someone else in two minutes and they’d be fine with it, it’s probably good enough. If I’d have to re-do it all over again for them, then maybe not. That’s the test I use for slides and reports.

---

**5. The Code compiles. The data looks right. But…**
If it’s code, I run it three times. If it’s a chart, I print it out and squint at it from the back of the room. If it’s a feeling, I walk away and come back in an hour. If it still feels off, I go back. But if I can’t tell the difference from last time, I stop.

---

**6. The clock’s not my friend**
I set a timer. If it’s done or it’s broken, I stop. If the timer’s halfway and I’m still not sure, I stop. There’s no sense in burning another minute on a maybe.

---

**7. The boss or the client would have to know it was broken**
If I can’t point to one thing and say, “that’s the only thing that could mess it up,” then it’s not done. If I can’t even say that, it’s not done.

---

So, it’s not about the numbers. It’s about if the doubt is eating me or the person who needs it. If I can’t sleep over it, I fix it. If I can, I move on. That’s when it’s good enough.

Giving critical feedback to someone who outranks you feels even more risky—every word could echo in their ear, and they’re the one who signed the approval forms. But skipping it or letting it fester is worse. Here’s how to do it right, so it’s about fixing the thing, not my reputation.

**1. Breathe. And mean it this time. I know you’ve heard it a hundred times, but I say it anyway. Steady hands, steady voice.**

**2. Frame it as the process, not the person. “The numbers didn’t look right at the end of step three,” not “you messed up step three.”**

**3. Use the data, not the gut. Show me the screen, show me the chart. If it’s wrong, it’s wrong. If it’s wrong twice, it’s wrong. That’s all I need.**

**4. Make three copies. One for me, one for them, one for the next guy who’ll have to fix it. I want to see it from every angle.**

**5. Say it slow, like I’m saying it to the client. “If we re-run the cycle at 7:30, it’ll be green, not red. I can do it now or we lose the whole batch.” That’s what happened. That’s what could happen again. That’s the only thing that matters.**

**6. Offer the fix, not just the failure. “If I rerun it now, it’ll take ten minutes and we’re good. If we wait till tomorrow, we lose the whole lot. I can show you the log if you want to check.”**

**7. Ask if they want to see the raw numbers. Let them look. Maybe it’s their screen, maybe it’s their eyes that missed it. But I double-checked twice. That’s the rule.**

**8. If they say no, then I write it in the log and tell the next guy. That’s the rule. But if they say yes, then we fix it together. That’s the rule.**

**9. If they start yelling at me, I just keep my hands on the keyboard and wait for them to sign off. I know what I saw. I saw it three times. That’s all that counts.**

**10. After we fix it, I send the new numbers to the boss and the client. I don’t say sorry. I just say “fixed.” That’s all anyone needs to know.**

If you can’t say it, you can’t fix it. And if you don’t fix it, you’re the one who’s wrong. That’s the only thing that counts.

Great question—this is a classic distinction in leadership studies and organizational behavior. Positional power and legitimate authority are often side by side in a chart or a flowchart, but they’re not the same thing. Here’s how I see it:

**Positional Power** is what someone has because of the title, the office, the signature, the badge, the name on the door. It’s the law that says “if you wear this, you can stop them.” It’s the right to make people do something because the system says so. But it doesn’t mean anyone has to.

**Legitimate Authority**, though, is about *why* people will do what you say. It’s not just because the badge says “supervisor.” It’s because everyone in the room knows why this matters, why it has to be done this way, and who to ask if they don’t understand. It’s the right because the process is right, the rules are clear, and everyone knows the difference between following the rule and breaking it. It’s not just a form to sign—it’s the reason behind the form.

So, the difference is in the *reason* people listen. Positional power is the lock on the door. Legitimate authority is the sign on the door that says why we’re all standing here, and if you don it, you know exactly what to do and why. That’s what makes people say yes, not just shake their head and look at the clock. That’s the difference that makes a manager who’s watched and learned, not just someone with a name on a piece of paper.

If you want a quick test: if someone could just turn around and do it again tomorrow without anyone blinking, it’s positional power. If everyone in the room knows what happens if it’s wrong, and why, and who’s responsible for fixing it, that’s legitimate authority.

1. **Read it all the way through.**  
   I’d make sure I understand every clause, the exceptions, the deadlines, and what’s supposed to happen if someone messes up. Missing something in the fine print could cost me later.

2. **Check the source.**  
   Is this in the main system? An email from HR? A form on the portal? I’d double-check where it came from and who approved it. Sometimes things get copied wrong or left out.

3. **See if there’s a reason.**  
   I’d look for the “why” behind it—what’s the point of this rule? Is it to stop someone from losing data? To save time? If I can’t see it, maybe it’s worth asking.

4. **Check the rules before.**  
   Is this new? Or did someone just forget to tell us about the old one? Old policies might still be in effect, and new ones can be mistakes.

5. **Talk to someone who already did it.**  
   If I can, I’d ask a teammate who’s done it before. They might know a loophole or a story about how it was supposed to work last year.

6. I’d write it down, exactly as it is, in my own words.  
   That way, if I get it wrong later, I know. And if I have to explain it to someone else, I won’t be the one who missed a step.

7. **Check the consequences.**  
   What happens if I don’t do it right? What if I do? Is there a form to fill out, a signature I have to get? If it’s just a box ticked, maybe it’s worth the risk. If it’s someone’s job to check, I’ll make sure I’ve got the proof.

8. **Look for a way to ask, not a way to say no.**  
   I’d phrase it as “Can you show me the checklist again? Last time it was this, and I want to be sure.” That way it’s about making sure I’m following, not about breaking the rule.

   Better to get it wrong once and fix it than mess up the whole batch. If I can’t be 100% sure, I’ll do it the first time right and flag it for review after.

That’s a really good question—those moments always feel like the whole room’s breathing wrong. When informal expertise, the gut feeling of someone who’s done it wrong last year, or the chat in the break room, says something different than the procedure in the manual or the manager’s checklist, it’s a real fork in the road. Here’s how I try to handle it, and some things to think about:

**1. Don’t just nod. Look.**  
I check both sides. I’ll re-read the steps, I’ll ask the person who did it last time if they still swear by it, and I’ll see if the form says one way and the logbook says another. Sometimes the paper’s right, sometimes the guy in the hoodie in the corner knows why.

**2. Ask the right people.**  
Not the boss, not the new guy. The person who actually did it last week, the one who almost burned the floor down last time. They remember the little things. Their hands remember the wrong way. If they say it’s fine, I listen. If they won’t touch it, I ask why.

**3. Write it down.**  
I get the forms, I get the notes, I get the photos. Sometimes the process is right, but the note says “don’t trust it,” and that’s the only proof. If I can’t get it on paper, I can’t say I did it right.

**4. Tell the boss, but not before I check the notes.**  
If I’m sure the form’s wrong and everyone knows, I bring it up after I’ve checked twice. If I just go off the chat, I’ll be the one who burned it. If I go by the form and the guy in the corner knows it’ll blow up, I’ll be the one who says it’s fine and it does. That’s not my job.

**5. If it can’t be fixed right now, I do what I know will keep it from blowing up.**  
That’s the rule. If the fire’s almost here and I can’t call it again, I do what I can and I write it down so it doesn’t happen next time. That’s the only honest way.

**6. After, I fix the notes.**  
If I cut it close, I tell the next person what actually happened. That’s how you don’t get the same mess twice. If the form’s wrong, I cross it out and write what I did, and I tell the boss. That’s the only way I sleep.

So, it’s not about trusting the gut or the book. It’s about knowing who knows what’s still burning, and making sure the next time it’s not me.

What about you? How do you decide?

1. **Stay Calm and Listen Carefully.**  
First, I make sure I hear the whole question before I answer. Sometimes they ask because they saw something, not because it’s wrong—so I wait until they finish.

2. **Clarify the Exact Question.**  
I restate what they’re asking, in my own words, so I’m sure I know what they’re looking at. If I’m unsure, I ask for the reference or the page number. That shows I’m organized.

3. **Check My Notes and the Source.**  
I go back to my records, the original calculations, the forms, the templates—I double-check everything. Maybe I missed a line or a date, so I go over it again.

4. **Explain the Method, Not Just the Answer.**  
I tell them exactly how I did it, from start to finish. If I used a formula, I show the formula and how I got the numbers. If I cross-referenced something, I show the source. I don’t just give the answer; I show how I got there.

5. **Ask Why, If I’m Not Sure.**

6. **Walk Through Every Step.**  
I go through the process again, out loud if I can, so they see exactly where I put the numbers in, how I moved them, what I checked. I keep a copy of the work right there so I can point to it.

7. **Show the Supporting Docs.**  
If I can, I pull the original receipts, the scan of the invoice, the approval—anything that backs it up. I lay it all out for them.

1. **Be early.** Show up when you said you would. Punctuality says you respect their time, and that’s the first thing you can’t miss.

2. **Say what’s true.** If I can’t do something, I say so before I promise. If something changes, I update everyone right away. Not making up stories or pretending things are fine when they’re not—that’s the fastest way to lose trust.

3. **Break the work into pieces.** If I can’t get it all done in one go, I tell them. And I do the first part myself. That way, they see I’m not just talking about it.

4. double-check my numbers. I don the same math twice. If I’m wrong, I own it and fix it. Not everyone does that.

5. ask them how they want things done. If they say “no, this is the way,” I do it their way, even if it’s slower. It’s the only way I know we both leave the right end line.

6. remember the little stuff. If they forget to sign something, I remind them. If they miss a file in the folder, I send it again. Those things add up to showing I’m looking out for the details.

7. and I keep my mouth shut when I don’t know. If I can’t say for sure, I say nothing. Guessing and then being wrong again? That’s another line in the sand.

You don’t have to be best friends or like each other to start clean. Just show up, do what I say I’ll do, and keep my hands clean when the dust settles. That’s how the ground stays level for the next thing.

This is a classic tension—people want to help, but if they’re always there, they never get the deep work they need. Here’s how to keep both things moving without one killing the other.

**1. Make it explicit.**  
Tell people what hours are for real work and what’s for questions or quick stuff. If you block 9–11 sharp for no interruptions, say it. If you’ll check messages after noon, say that. Clarity saves you from explaining twice.

**2. Use a to-do list that can’t be done.**  
Before I start any real project, I lock it in my head and write it down. If someone asks for a thing that could bleed into this, I say no unless it’s in the next two hours and I can do it in one go. That’s the rule. If it’s not, it goes back to the queue.

**3. Schedule “help hours.”**  
Twelve noon to two, I’ll answer anything that’s burning. But if it’s just another thing that’ll turn into three things, I say no. That way, people know when to wait and when to send it to the queue.

**4. Use a timer.**  
I set a timer for 90 minutes, then 15 minutes off. If someone drops a question during those 90, I write it down and forget it. If it’s urgent, they have to wait. That’s the only way I’ll check anything during the work time. After the timer, I see the list and decide what’s actually done.

**5. Make it easy for them to know.**  
I keep a doc with my hours and the rules. If someone asks, they see it. If they don’t, they learn next time. It’s better than guessing.

**6. Say no to meetings.**  
If I have a block, I don’t. If someone wants to talk about their stupid spreadsheet, I say tomorrow at noon. If it’s not on the list, it doesn’t get done. That’s the rule.

**7. Trust people to remember.**  
If they need something urgent, they can ping me after the timer. If it’s not urgent, it waits. I’m not the only one who can’t juggle twenty things at once.

**8. If you can’t say no, at least say why.**  
I tell people exactly why I can’t help now. If it’s not the cut-off, I’ll do it after. If it’s because I’m in the middle of something that can’t split, I say so. That way, they learn when to send it again.

**9. Make the queue public.**  
If someone keeps pinging for stuff that’s not in the right slot, I put it on a to-do and remind them it’s not moving until the block is done. That way, they know where it is.

**10. At the end of the day, I check the list.**  
If I missed something because someone bugged me, I own it and fix it before I close. But if it’s their fault for not tagging it right, I tell them next time.

It’s not perfect, but it keeps the chaos out of my work time and lets people know when they can actually help. If you do it for a week, it’ll stick.
